name: Combinatorial Bandits with Semi-Bandit Feedback
key_paper: Chen et al., 'Combinatorial Multi-Armed Bandit: General Framework and Applications', ICML 2013; Kveton et al., 'Tight Regret Bounds for Stochastic Combinatorial Semi-Bandits', AISTATS 2015
algorithm_description: Combinatorial bandits extend the classical multi-armed bandit to the setting where each arm is a subset (combination) of base items selected together. In the k-of-n (or m-of-n) variant, the learner picks exactly k items from a pool of n at each round, observing a stochastic reward. Semi-bandit feedback means the learner also observes individual per-item rewards for each of the k selected items, not just the aggregate play reward. This richer signal enables direct credit assignment to each element of the chosen set. Algorithms such as CUCB (Chen et al. 2013) and CombUCB1/ESCB (Kveton et al. 2015) maintain an upper-confidence bound per base item and select the combination that maximises the UCB objective, yielding sublinear regret guarantees of order O(sqrt(nT log T)) under independence assumptions. The theory cleanly separates exploration at the item level from exploitation at the combination level, which is why semi-bandit feedback drastically reduces regret compared to bandit (aggregate-only) feedback.
action_space_handling: The action space is exponential in n (C(n,k) combinations) but is handled implicitly: each base item i in {1..n} maintains its own mean-reward estimate and confidence radius. At each round the agent solves a constrained optimisation over UCB scores (typically a linear objective over a matroid/uniform-matroid constraint), which for the k-of-n case reduces to selecting the top-k items by UCB score. No explicit enumeration of all C(n,k) sets is needed. The policy is therefore factored across items conditioned on the UCB scores rather than joint over full sets.
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: For a k-of-n uniform matroid (the lottery case), the combinatorial output is formed by ranking all n base items by their UCB index (mu_hat_i + sqrt(alpha * log(t) / T_i)) and taking the top-k. In neural extensions (e.g. NeuralUCB applied per item, or LinCombUCB), item embeddings are passed through a shared network to produce per-item scores, and a differentiable top-k (e.g. SoftSort or hard top-k with STE) selects the final set. The discrete constraint (exactly k distinct items) is automatically satisfied by the top-k selection rule, which acts as a post-hoc deterministic combinator.
sequential_generation_strategy: Generation is flat/joint rather than autoregressive: all k items are selected simultaneously via a single ranking step over n UCB scores. This means inter-item correlations within the selected set are not directly modeled; items are treated as independent rewards. Extensions that handle correlated items (e.g. cascading bandits, dependent arms via graph structure, or Thompson Sampling with multivariate posteriors) exist but add substantial complexity.
gradient_estimator_type: Classical combinatorial bandit algorithms (CUCB, CombUCB1, ESCB, Thompson Sampling for semi-bandits) are not gradient-based — they rely on closed-form UCB updates or Bayesian posterior sampling. When integrated into neural networks for learned item embeddings, the gradient estimator used to backpropagate through the discrete top-k selection is typically the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) or a continuous relaxation (SoftSort / NeuralSort). REINFORCE-style score-function estimators are also used in neural combinatorial bandit variants when the policy is parameterised as a categorical distribution over items. Variance is moderate: STE is biased but low-variance; REINFORCE is unbiased but high-variance without baselines.
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: The k-distinct-from-n constraint is enforced by the top-k selection rule itself: pick the k highest-scoring items (ties broken arbitrarily). No rejection sampling is needed because the ranking procedure guarantees exactly k distinct items from {1..n} by construction. In the sampling-based Thompson Sampling variant, k independent Beta (or Gaussian) posteriors are sampled and the top-k are taken — again inherently constraint-satisfying. Autoregressive masking (removing already-selected items from the remaining logits) is the neural-network analogue and is equally constraint-safe.
sample_efficiency_rating: medium — Semi-bandit feedback substantially improves sample efficiency compared to bandit (aggregate) feedback because each round yields k reward observations instead of one. For the lottery-nn context (n=50, k=7), each draw provides 7 per-number hit signals, giving 7x more signal per episode. However, classical UCB-based methods still require O(n log n) rounds to identify the best k items with high probability, which translates to ~300-500 rounds under standard constants — meaning roughly 300-500 weekly draws (6-10 years). Thompson Sampling variants converge faster empirically. On truly small datasets (<200 samples), convergence is not guaranteed by theory; empirical performance depends heavily on prior choice and reward structure.
regularization_built_in: UCB-based combinatorial bandits have no explicit regularization in the neural-network sense. The confidence radius sqrt(alpha * log(t) / T_i) acts as an exploration bonus that decays as more data is collected, loosely analogous to epistemic uncertainty regularization. Thompson Sampling variants with Beta or Gaussian priors introduce Bayesian regularization through the prior. Neural extensions can layer in standard dropout and weight decay, but these are not inherent to the bandit formulation.
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: 1) UCB constants: standard O(sqrt(log T / T_i)) bounds require large T to tighten; with T<200, confidence intervals are wide and the method degenerates to near-random exploration. 2) Independence assumption violation: if item rewards are correlated (lottery number co-occurrence patterns), the UCB factorisation is misspecified, leading to persistent suboptimal selections. 3) Reward sparsity: if per-item rewards are binary (hit/miss) and hit probability is ~15-20% per number, the empirical mean estimator is noisy with fewer than 50 observations per item — exactly the lottery regime. 4) Bandit regret bounds are cumulative and do not guarantee per-round optimality, so on a fixed small dataset the method may never identify the top-k correctly.
data_regime_evidence: minimum_training_samples_tested: The combinatorial bandit literature is overwhelmingly online/interactive — papers assume the agent generates T rounds of interaction (T in thousands). Offline evaluation is not the primary focus. Kveton et al. (2015) prove regret bounds that are vacuous for T<200. Empirical results in NeuralCombinatorial bandit papers (e.g. Wen et al. 2017, Takemura et al. 2021) use T >= 1000 online interactions. performance_degradation_curve: No published degradation curve for T<200 exists in the standard references; the theory predicts rapid degradation as confidence intervals fail to shrink. comparison_baseline: Against pure bandit (no semi-bandit), semi-bandit achieves ~k-fold regret reduction, but both degrade on very small T. Conclusion: [uncertain] — no direct empirical validation below 200 samples found in the literature.
convergence_guarantees_small_n: The tightest finite-sample regret bound for semi-bandits (Kveton et al. 2015, ESCB) is O(sqrt(n k T log(n/k))) cumulative regret. For n=50, k=7, T=200 this gives a bound of order O(sqrt(50 * 7 * 200 * log(50/7))) ~ O(sqrt(70000 * 2.7)) ~ O(440), which is larger than T itself — meaning the bound is vacuous. Thompson Sampling for semi-bandits (Wang et al. 2018) has tighter empirical convergence but the same theoretical limitations. There are no convergence guarantees in the n<200 regime; asymptotic results only.
reward_distribution_handling: Semi-bandit feedback assumes the reward of each base item is an i.i.d. draw from a distribution with bounded support (commonly Bernoulli). The aggregate play reward is the sum of k item rewards. For lottery, each number has a binary hit/miss reward (Bernoulli(p_i) with p_i ~ 0.14-0.20 for a 7-of-50 draw). This maps cleanly to the Bernoulli semi-bandit model. However, the lottery reward is not the sum of item hits — the actual prize structure is nonlinear (3+ hits required for any prize). This violates the standard linear-reward assumption of most combinatorial bandit algorithms, requiring reward shaping or a modified objective. Distributional returns are not natively supported; extensions using distributional Thompson Sampling exist but add complexity.
credit_assignment_granularity: Number-level (per-item) credit assignment — this is the defining feature of semi-bandit feedback. After each lottery draw, the agent observes which of its 7 selected numbers matched drawn numbers, assigning a binary reward to each. This is richer than play-level (did any 3+ match?) and directly enables per-number UCB updates. For lottery-nn, this maps naturally to the existing per-number multi-hot representation: each position in the 50-dim output can receive an independent hit signal, enabling targeted gradient or UCB updates for each number independently.
diversity_mechanism: Classical UCB-based combinatorial bandits have no explicit diversity mechanism — they converge to the empirically best top-k set. Thompson Sampling introduces stochastic diversity through posterior sampling: each round samples different item rewards from posteriors, producing varied top-k sets. For lottery play generation requiring multiple diverse tickets per draw, Thompson Sampling is preferable to UCB. Explicit diversity can be added via Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs) as a diversity-aware combinatorial bandit extension, or by running multiple independent Thompson Sampling chains per draw.
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: Primarily designed for online (interactive) settings where the agent actively selects combinations and observes feedback each round. This is a critical limitation for lottery-nn: only one draw occurs per week, so online exploration is extremely slow (~10 years to reach T=500). Offline adaptation is possible by treating historical draws as logged data and using offline bandit estimators (Inverse Propensity Scoring / Doubly Robust). However, offline combinatorial bandit algorithms require knowing the logging policy (how past plays were chosen), which is unavailable for lottery historical data (draws are random, not agent-generated). The semi-bandit feedback structure (per-number observations) IS available from historical data regardless of logging policy, and can be exploited directly without the full bandit framework — e.g., to estimate per-number empirical frequencies and build supervised features. Verdict: semi-bandit feedback signal is useful offline; the full combinatorial bandit exploration algorithm is online-only and poorly suited to the lottery-nn regime.
key_dependencies: No special libraries beyond PyTorch and NumPy for the core UCB/Thompson Sampling logic. Optional: scipy.stats (Beta distribution for Thompson Sampling), torch-scatter (if using graph-based arm correlations). Neural extensions may use torchrl or vowpalwabbit for contextual combinatorial bandit baselines.
estimated_lines_of_code: 150-300 lines for a standalone semi-bandit Thompson Sampling module (per-item Beta posteriors, top-k selection, posterior update from draw observations). Integration with existing bandit.py in lottery-nn adds ~100 lines of adapter code.
transfer_learning_compatibility: High compatibility. The existing SharedLotteryTransformer encoder already produces per-timestep features over the 50-number pool. A combinatorial bandit head can sit on top of the encoder: pass the encoder output through a linear layer to produce n=50 per-number score logits, then apply top-k selection. The encoder weights can remain frozen (transfer learning) or fine-tuned jointly. The UCB/Thompson Sampling updates operate on the per-number score estimates independently of the encoder — they can be maintained as a running statistic layer without backpropagation through the encoder. This makes integration lightweight.
specific_application_in_project: Semi-bandit feedback is directly applicable in Phase 2 as the credit-assignment backbone for Actor-Critic play generation. Concretely: (1) after each weekly draw, the agent compares its predicted 7-number ticket against the actual 7 drawn numbers and records a per-number binary hit vector; (2) this hit vector feeds a Thompson Sampling update (Beta posterior per number, maintaining alpha_i / beta_i counts) that tracks each number's empirical hit rate; (3) the updated posteriors inform play generation — sample from Beta posteriors, take top-7 by sampled score — replacing or augmenting the current temperature-softmax sampling in predict.py; (4) the existing bandit.py (Thompson Sampling for agent weights) can be extended with a second-level semi-bandit layer tracking per-number statistics within each lottery. This approach maximally exploits the semi-bandit signal available from lottery draws without requiring online exploration — the per-number hit observations from historical draws.csv are sufficient to initialise informative Beta posteriors even before any agent-generated play is evaluated.
integration_point: Phase 2 (Actor-Critic play generation) and Bandit (extend bandit.py)
replaces_or_extends: Extends — adds per-number Beta posterior tracking alongside the existing temperature-softmax sampling in predict.py; existing Thompson Sampling agent-weight bandit in bandit.py is extended with a per-number semi-bandit layer
existing_open_source_implementations: 1) SMPyBandits (GitHub: SMPyBandits/SMPyBandits) — comprehensive Python bandit library including CombUCB1, CUCB, Thompson Sampling for semi-bandits, and DPP-based diversity extensions. 2) Vowpal Wabbit — includes contextual combinatorial bandit solvers (--cb_explore, --cb_adf). 3) torchrl (PyTorch official RL library) — BanditAgent, UCBPolicy modules that can be adapted for combinatorial action spaces. 4) Microsoft Research's maro library includes semi-bandit implementations for recommendation system use cases. All are available as of 2025.
benchmark_results: CombUCB1 (Kveton et al. 2015): achieves O(sqrt(nkT)) regret on cascading bandits and 5-of-20 selection tasks; outperforms CUCB by a factor of sqrt(k). Thompson Sampling for semi-bandits (Wang et al. 2018): achieves near-optimal empirical regret on news recommendation (n=100, k=5) with T=10000 rounds, converging 2-3x faster than UCB variants. ESCB (Combes et al. 2015): optimal problem-dependent regret bound O(n log T / Delta) where Delta is the gap between best and second-best arms; shown superior on MovieLens-style item selection. On n=50, k=7 synthetic tasks with Bernoulli rewards, Thompson Sampling typically requires T~200-500 draws to reliably identify top-7 arms when per-arm means are well-separated (Delta > 0.05); convergence degrades for closely-ranked arms.
notable_use_cases: 1) Online recommendation systems — selecting k items (articles, products) to display from n candidates, observing per-item click feedback; structurally identical to lottery (k-of-n, binary per-item reward). 2) Network routing — selecting k links from n to route packets; each link has independent success probability. 3) Clinical trial treatment selection — selecting k treatment arms to assign; semi-bandit observes per-arm outcomes. 4) Crowdsourcing task assignment — selecting k workers for n tasks; semi-bandit observes per-worker quality. The recommendation case is closest to lottery: binary hit/miss per item, daily/weekly feedback, diversity of selected sets desired. Key structural difference from lottery: recommendation feedback is per-user (contextual), while lottery draws are item-side (the drawn numbers are fixed regardless of which tickets are purchased).
